Division produces collapse: a house divided against itself cannot stand. If Satan is casting out his own agents, his kingdom is in terminal self-destruction. But nothing in the evidence suggests that; on the contrary, it is being invaded and plundered by an external force.

The ‘strong man’ image is one of the most powerful metaphors in the gospels. Satan is the strong man who has kept his house secure — humanity under his dominion. Jesus is the stronger one who has entered, bound the strong man, and is plundering his goods — rescuing the people the strong man held captive. Every exorcism in Mark is an act of plunder. Every healing is a reclamation. The kingdom of God advances not by negotiation but by conquest.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, all sins will be forgiven the children of man, and whatever blasphemies they utter, but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin — for they were saying, ‘He has an unclean spirit.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is one of the most solemnly stated passages in Mark, and one of the most misunderstood. The statement is framed with ‘truly’ (amēn) — the authoritative formula Mark uses for Jesus’s most significant pronouncements. The breadth of divine forgiveness is established first: all sins, all blasphemies, will be forgiven the children of man. The mercy of God is panoramic. And then the exception, stated with equal solemnity: but blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven, in this age or the age to come. An eternal sin.

Mark’s explanation is precise (v. 30): the context is the scribes’ accusation that Jesus casts out demons by Beelzebul. This is not merely false doctrine or confused theology; it is the deliberate, determined attribution of the Spirit’s work to Satan. The Holy Spirit was visibly, unambiguously at work — the exorcisms were real, the deliverances were happening before their eyes — and the scribes, in full knowledge of what they were seeing, chose to call it demonic. This is not an error of ignorance; it is the sin of the person who looks at the light and calls it darkness, who sees the Holy Spirit’s power and names it the devil’s.

The pastoral question this verse has raised throughout church history is: can I have committed this sin? R. C. Sproul notes the telling answer: the person who fears they have committed the unforgivable sin almost certainly has not. The very anxiety is evidence of a conscience still alive, still responsive to the Spirit, still capable of grief over sin. The unforgivable sin is not committed in a moment of weakness or doubt; it is the settled, hardened, final attribution of the Spirit’s work to Satan by people who know exactly what they are doing. The scribes in this passage are the type: they have seen the evidence and they have chosen their verdict, and they have chosen it in conscious defiance of what they know to be true. cf. Matt. 12:31–32; 1 John 5:16

verseByVerse.quote: And looking about at those who sat around him, he said, ‘Here are my mother and my brothers! Whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The arrival of Jesus’s family must be read in light of verse 21, where his family went to seize him, saying he was out of his mind. They are coming not to support but to pull him back — interrupting what they consider a public embarrassment. His mother and brothers are on the outside of the crowd: even those physically closest to Jesus are not automatically on the inside of the kingdom.

Jesus’s response is not a rejection of his family — he provides for his mother from the cross (John 19:26–27). It is a redefinition: the deepest bond is not biological but covenantal. ‘Whoever does the will of God’ — the new family constituted by obedience and faith. This is the gospel’s social revolution: a new family gathered not by birth but by rebirth, not by blood but by the blood of the new covenant.

3.theology:
Chapter 3 presents the paradox at the heart of Jesus’s ministry: the more he is opposed by the religious establishment, the wider the circle of those who come to him. The Pharisee-Herodian alliance forms in verse 6; the crowds from across the entire region form in verses 7–8; the Twelve are appointed in verses 13–19; the scribes accuse in verses 22–30. Opposition and expansion move together — a pattern that runs through the entire New Testament and church history.

The Beelzebul controversy introduces the cosmic dimension of Jesus’s ministry present since the temptation (1:12–13). The exorcisms are battles in a war. Jesus has entered Satan’s territory, bound the strong man, and is taking back what was stolen. The kingdom of God advances not through argument alone but through authority — the authority of the one who conquered the strong man.
3.examples: The unforgivable sin passage (vv. 28–30) has caused tremendous anxiety for sensitive consciences across the centuries. The sin described is not a moment of doubt or a blasphemous thought that crossed an exhausted mind; it is the sustained, deliberate, calculating attribution of the Spirit’s unmistakable work to the devil. The person genuinely afraid of having committed it almost certainly has not: that fear is itself the evidence of a conscience still alive. Bunyan’s Pilgrim carries this fear for much of the journey, and Bunyan’s counsel is wise: the very burden of the fear is proof that grace is still at work.

4.title: Hearing, Seeing, and the Stilling of the Storm
4.text: "He said to them, 'Do you not yet understand?'" (Mark 4:40 ESV — the disciples after the storm)
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the only extended teaching section in Mark's gospel. Everywhere else Jesus acts; here he pauses at the lakeside and explains. The parable of the sower is the master key to all the parables — Jesus says so explicitly (v. 13). If you understand the sower, you can read the rest. But the chapter ends not with understanding but with fear: the disciples, having heard all the parables, are terrified by the storm and astonished when Jesus stills it. They still do not understand who is in the boat with them. The gap between hearing and understanding is the theme of the whole chapter.

The parable of the sower is also, read carefully, a parable about itself. It is a story about how stories are received — and it predicts its own mixed reception. Some will hear and not understand; some will receive with joy and fall away; some will allow the word to be choked out; and some will produce a harvest. The parable does not despair over the shallow soil and the thorns. The sower keeps sowing. The point is the harvest that is coming, not the losses along the way. The kingdom begins small and hidden — a seed, a lamp under a basket — but its ending is certain and abundant.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Parable of the Sower and the Purpose of Parables
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The parable of the sower is told beside the Sea of Galilee to an enormous crowd, with Jesus teaching from a boat. The setting itself is a kind of parable: the word going out from a single source, received differently by the different soils it lands on. Mark then records a private explanation given to the disciples and the inner circle — one of the only moments in Mark where Jesus explains a parable in detail.

The purpose of parables statement (vv. 10–12) is one of the most debated passages in Mark. Jesus seems to be saying that the parables are designed to prevent outsiders from understanding. The background is Isaiah 6:9–10, where the prophet is told to speak to a people who will hear but not understand, see but not perceive. Jesus is not being arbitrary or cruel; he is describing the effect that a self-hardened heart has when it encounters veiled truth. The parables are mercy: they keep the truth available to those who seek, while preserving it from those who would only use it to condemn themselves further.
verseByVerse.theology: The four soils represent four responses to the word of God, and they are not merely historical types but living possibilities in every congregation on every Sunday. The path: the word heard and immediately taken. The rocky ground: received with joy, abandoned when the cost becomes real. The thorny ground: accepted alongside the word but eventually strangling it — 'the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches and the desires for other things' (v. 19). And the good soil: receiving the word, holding it, bearing fruit — thirtyfold, sixtyfold, a hundredfold. The question the parable poses to every hearer is not 'which soil do I hope I am?' but 'which soil am I?' That question can only be answered by looking at what the word has actually produced in your life.
verseByVerse.examples: 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear' (v. 9) — this refrain appears throughout the teaching of Jesus and recurs seven times in the letters to the churches in Revelation 2–3. It is an invitation to go beyond mere acoustic reception to genuine spiritual reception. Physical hearing is universal; spiritual hearing is the miracle. Every preacher knows both soils in the same congregation: the person in the front row whose life the word has permeated, and the person in the same row who has heard a thousand sermons and is unchanged. The difference is not the quality of the preaching but the condition of the soil. And the condition of the soil — here is the mercy — can change.

verseByVerse.quote: And he was teaching them many things in parables, and in his teaching he said to them: 'Listen! Behold, a sower went out to sow. And as he sowed, some seed fell along the path… other seeds fell into good soil and produced grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parable of the sower is not primarily about the sower or about the sowing — it is about the soils. The sower's method is unchanged from the first seed to the last: he sows everywhere, lavishly, without pre-sorting the ground. The word of the kingdom goes out to all without prior selection. The outcomes differ not because the seed differs but because the soils differ. This is the key to understanding both the variety of human responses to the gospel and the confidence of the sower: the soil problem is real, but the harvest is also real and overwhelming.

A hundredfold harvest is extraordinary — normal yields in Palestine were fivefold to tenfold. The extravagance of the good soil's harvest is the point. The losses — the path, the rocks, the thorns — are acknowledged but not dwelt on. The parable is ultimately not about the three failed soils but about the one that succeeded beyond all reasonable expectation. The kingdom of God, despite its apparent fragility and mixed reception, will produce a harvest that exceeds all expectation.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he was alone, those around him with the twelve asked him about the parables. And he said to them, 'To you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God, but for those outside everything is in parables, so that they may indeed see but not perceive, and may indeed hear but not understand, lest they should turn and be forgiven.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The quotation from Isaiah 6:9–10 is not a statement of divine cruelty but of judicial hardening — the same principle Paul expounds in Romans 9–11. Those who have consistently refused the light find themselves increasingly unable to see by it. The parables are simultaneously revealing and concealing: revealing to those who come with seeking hearts (to them the secret of the kingdom is given), concealing to those who have hardened themselves against the word. Truth veiled in story keeps seeking hearts seeking without delivering self-condemning knowledge to those who would only weaponize it.

The disciples are on the inside — not because they are spiritually superior but because they are genuinely seeking. They ask. That asking is itself the evidence of the 'given' that verse 11 describes. The secret of the kingdom is given to those who want it enough to ask for it.

Still, Mark's wording is harder than a first reading lets on, and it should not be smoothed over. Matthew says Jesus speaks in parables 'because' people do not see (Matt 13:13); Mark says he speaks so that ('in order that') they may not see, 'lest they should turn and be forgiven.' Read flatly, that sounds as though Jesus veils the truth deliberately to keep people from repenting. Three things dissolve the difficulty. First, the words are a direct quotation of Isaiah 6:9-10, God's charge to a prophet sent to a nation that had already, for generations, shut its eyes; this is not fresh cruelty but the settled judgment of God on hardened refusal. Second, the 'in order that' carries the weight of fulfilment as much as bare purpose — the parables come to a people who have chosen blindness, and confirm the choice; God gives them over to the dark they preferred (cf. Rom 1:24). Third, and crucially, the door is never bolted: the very people 'around him with the twelve' understood nothing either — until they asked. To everyone who asks, the secret is given. So the same parable is judgment and mercy at once: it hardens the scornful and it shelters the seeker, hiding the truth from the mouth that would only spit on it while keeping it within reach of any who will turn.

verseByVerse.quote: 'The sower sows the word. And these are the ones along the path, where the word is sown: when they hear, Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that is sown in them… But those that were sown on the good soil are the ones who hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus's interpretation of the sower is the only detailed allegorical interpretation of a parable in Mark. Each soil is identified: the path (v. 15) — Satan immediately removes the word; no understanding, no retention. The rocky ground (vv. 16–17) — immediate joy, but no root; tribulation or persecution 'on account of the word' causes immediate falling away. Note the phrase: the testing is specifically because of the word. The Thorny ground (vv. 18–19) — the word is received, but it competes with the cares of the world, the deceitfulness of riches, and desires for other things. The word is not rejected; it is choked. The good soil (v. 20) — hears, accepts, bears fruit. The sequence matters: hearing leads to acceptance, acceptance leads to fruit. The fruit is not the goal that produces acceptance; the fruit is the natural outcome of genuine acceptance.

The three failed soils each represent a different way of losing the word: immediately (the path), in the first storm (rocky ground), and gradually over time through competition (thorny ground). The three are not stages — they are types. The examination this parable demands is honest self-assessment: where is my life producing fruit? Where has the word been taken, withered, or choked?

But the parable, pressed this way, frightens a certain kind of hearer — the tender, self-suspicious believer who reads the rocky and thorny ground and concludes he must be one of them, that his joy was shallow and his falling-away only a matter of time. So a gospel word must be added, or the parable is left to do harm it was never meant to do. First, the very anxiety is a hopeful sign. The path-hearer feels nothing; Satan takes the word and the man is undisturbed. The one genuinely afraid that he is unfruitful is not exhibiting the symptom of hard ground but of soil the word has reached and troubled — dead ground does not grieve its own barrenness. Second, and this is the mercy the parable does not state but the whole Bible supplies: your soil is not your fate. A field is not doomed to stay a footpath. The same God who sends the seed also breaks up the ground to receive it — ‘Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns’ (Jer 4:3; Hos 10:12) — and where the heart is hard beyond self-repair he promises to do the thing the soil cannot do for itself: ‘I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh’ (Ezek 36:26). No one reading this is fixed forever as path or rock or thorn.

And that turns the self-examination from despair into action, because the two middle soils name their own remedy. If the trouble is shallow roots that wither under heat, the answer is to sink roots now, in the cool of an ordinary week — into Scripture, prayer, and the company of God’s people — so that when the persecution or the trial comes there is something to draw on. If the trouble is thorns, the cares and riches and desires that crowd the word out, then the thorns must be named and cut: the specific anxiety, the specific love of money, the specific appetite that is choking the plant. This is not something you accomplish by straining to be better soil; it is asking the Sower himself, who breaks up fallow ground, to do in you what you cannot do in yourself — and then living toward the answer. The parable ends not in verdict but in hope: the harvest is still coming, and the God who gives the growth is not finished with your field.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Is a lamp brought in to be put under a basket, or under a bed, and not on a stand? For nothing is hidden except to be made manifest; nor is anything secret except to come to light… For to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lamp saying (vv. 21–22) connects to the parable of the sower: the hiddenness of the parables is temporary, not permanent. Nothing is hidden except to be made manifest. The Messianic Secret, the veiled teaching, the seed growing in secret — all of these are temporary concealments of what is eventually and fully revealed. The lamp is not permanently under the basket; it is placed there for a season, and then it is put on the stand.

'Pay attention to what you hear' (v. 24) — the measure you give (of attention, of receptivity, of openness) is the measure you receive. The spiritual economics of the kingdom run opposite to the economics of the world: in the kingdom, use produces increase, and non-use produces loss. The person who genuinely receives and acts on the word finds that more is given; the person who hears and does nothing finds that even the hearing fades.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–41 — The Growing Seed, the Mustard Seed, and the Storm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The two parables that follow (the seed growing secretly and the mustard seed) address the apparent smallness and invisibility of the kingdom's beginning. Both are parables of encouragement for a movement that appears far too small to matter. The seed grows while the farmer sleeps — the kingdom advances by a power not resident in the human agent. The mustard seed, smallest of seeds, becomes the largest of garden plants and shelters birds: the kingdom that begins in one man from Nazareth will eventually provide shelter for the nations.

The chapter closes with the storm on the lake — and the contrast between the sleeping Jesus and the terrified disciples is the chapter's climactic parable without being called one. They have heard the sower, the lamp, the growing seed, the mustard seed. And then they face a storm, and they are terrified, and they cry 'Don't you care that we are perishing?' — and Jesus rebukes both the wind and their unbelief.
verseByVerse.theology: The storm episode (vv. 35–41) is a theophany — a revelation of divine presence. When Jesus rebukes the wind and sea with a word and there is a great calm, the disciples' fear of the storm is replaced by a greater fear: 'Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?' The language echoes Psalm 107:25–30, where the LORD stills the storm and the waves. The disciples are not asking a merely academic question; they are beginning to confront the possibility that the person in their boat is the Lord of creation. This is the knowledge the parables have been preparing them for — but knowledge of this magnitude cannot be conveyed by instruction alone. It must be encountered in the storm.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus is asleep in the stern on a cushion while the storm rages — the most remarkable detail in the chapter. His sleep is not ignorance or indifference; it is the sleep of one who knows who is in command of the sea. The disciples, who have seen everything in chapters 1–3, still do not know who is in the boat with them. They wake him in panic. He rebukes the storm. Then he rebukes them: 'Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?' The order matters. He calms the storm first — because they need the calm — and then addresses the faith failure. Then: twelve disciples in a boat, terrified, with the Lord of wind and wave asleep four feet away. Now: every believer in the storm who forgets who is in the boat.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, 'The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.'
verseByVerse.commentary: This parable is unique to Mark. The farmer scatters seed and then — does nothing. He sleeps and rises, goes about his life, and the seed grows without him. 'He knows not how' — the kingdom's growth is not the product of human understanding or human effort. It happens by a power inherent in the word itself, in the soil that the Spirit has prepared. The farmer's job is to sow and then to trust. The harvest comes when the grain is ripe, and then the sickle is put in — an echo of Joel 3:13 and the language of eschatological harvest. The kingdom grows secretly, inevitably, toward a final harvest that is certain.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, 'With what can we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable shall we use for it? It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when sown on the ground, is the smallest of all the seeds on earth, yet when it is sown it grows up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mustard seed was proverbially small — the standard Jewish idiom for something tiny. The contrast between smallest-of-seeds and largest-of-garden-plants is maximized for effect. The birds nesting in its branches may echo Daniel 4:12, where the great tree shelters the nations under Nebuchadnezzar's dominion — and Daniel 4:21, where the birds of the air represent the nations. The image is of the kingdom that begins in Galilee ending by sheltering the whole world. This is the confidence the parables are designed to produce: the smallness of the beginning is no argument against the greatness of the ending.

Mark notes in vv. 33–34 that Jesus spoke the word to them in many parables, 'as they were able to hear it,' and explained everything privately to his disciples. The teaching is calibrated — not all truth is given at once. The disciples who hear the private explanation are being shaped slowly toward a truth that will only be fully comprehensible after the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: And a great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling. But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. And they woke him and said to him, 'Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?' And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, 'Peace! Be still!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sea of Galilee is notorious for sudden, violent storms — the lake sits some 600 feet below sea level in a basin surrounded by hills, and cold air can funnel down to create dangerous conditions with very little warning. These are experienced fishermen in their own boat on their own lake. Their terror is not weakness; the storm is genuinely life-threatening.

Jesus rebukes the wind and sea with the same vocabulary used throughout Mark for rebuking demons. The storm is addressed as a hostile force and it obeys — the same instant obedience the demonic spirits gave in the synagogue. The disciples' question — 'Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?' — is the right question. They do not yet have the answer. That answer is coming in a cross and an empty tomb. But they are asking it now, in a suddenly calm boat, with water dripping off the gunwales, and the answer will never leave them.

And their question is not left hanging in the air; the Scriptures they knew by heart already held the answer. In the Psalms the stilling of the sea is one thing and one thing only — a work of God himself: 'He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed' (Ps 107:29); 'You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them' (Ps 89:9); it was the LORD who 'shut in the sea with doors' and said, 'Thus far shall you come, and no farther' (Job 38:8-11). So 'who then is this?' has only one possible answer, and it is an answer that should have frightened them more than the storm did. The One asleep on the cushion, worn out like any man, is the One whose voice the sea has obeyed since the third day of creation. Fully man in his exhaustion, fully God in his word — and the disciples are beginning, dimly, to see it.

4.theology:
Chapter 4 establishes that the kingdom of God operates by a logic entirely different from the world's logic. It comes hidden, like a seed. It grows secretly, without human supervision. It starts small and ends immense. It is received differently by different people, and the difference lies not in the quality of the word but in the condition of the heart. And the one who brings this kingdom has authority over the creation itself — the wind and the sea obey him. These are not incidental details; they are the theological framework for everything that follows.

The chapter's final question — 'Who then is this?' — is the question Mark has been building toward since verse 1. The miracles, the teaching, the exorcisms, the controversies: all of them are pressing the reader toward this question. Who is this? The parables hint. The storm answers — partially. The full answer waits for chapter 8's confession at Caesarea Philippi and chapter 15's declaration at the foot of the cross.
4.examples: The three failed soils of the parable are not comfortable to preach because they are not comfortable to recognize. The rocky-ground hearer is the person who received the word with genuine joy — who came to Christ in a real moment of encounter — but who, when the cost came, left. The thorny-ground hearer is the person who never formally rejected the word but who allowed the pressures of life and the seductions of prosperity to crowd it out until the fruit stopped appearing. Both of these are more common in Western Christianity than the path hearer. The preacher who has the courage to press the parable with specific, concrete, contemporary illustrations of what the rocky ground and the thorny ground look like today is doing the most important thing that can be done with this text.

5.title: Three Miracles and the Power of Touch
5.text: "'Who touched my garments?' And his disciples said to him, 'You see the crowd pressing around you, and yet you say, Who touched me?'" (Mark 5:30–31 ESV)
5.overview:
Chapter 5 gives us three of the most intimate and detailed healing accounts in the gospels — and their intimacy is no accident, since they come from Peter's eyewitness memory. The Gerasene demoniac, the woman with the bleeding, and Jairus's daughter form a triptych of impossible situations: a man beyond human help, a woman beyond medical help, and a child beyond all help. Jesus meets all three. The structure of the chapter is itself a teaching device: the Jairus story begins, is interrupted by the woman's story, and then resumes — the classic Markan 'sandwich,' in which the interruption interprets the main narrative.

What the chapter collectively argues is that no situation is beyond the reach of this man. The demoniac is the most extreme case of possession in the gospels. The woman has been ill for twelve years and has spent everything on doctors. Jairus's daughter is dead by the time Jesus arrives. Each scenario is worse than the one before it. And the power of Jesus is equal to all three.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The crossing of the lake that ended with the storm (ch. 4) brings Jesus to Gentile territory — the Decapolis region on the eastern shore. He has barely stepped from the boat when he is met by a man who is, in every human sense, beyond recovery. He lives among the tombs, cries out day and night, cuts himself with stones, has broken every chain that men have put on him, and is possessed by so many demons that their name is 'Legion' — a Roman military term for approximately six thousand soldiers. The name is itself a clue: this is not a picture of ordinary demonic oppression but of an entire region held under satanic dominion, and Jesus has crossed the sea specifically to liberate it.

The liberation of this man is the most dramatic exorcism in the gospels. The demons recognize Jesus, acknowledge his authority, beg for mercy, and are permitted to enter a herd of two thousand pigs — which immediately rush into the sea and drown. The townspeople arrive to find the man clothed and in his right mind, and their reaction is not gratitude but fear. They ask Jesus to leave. The man who was saved begs to go with him; Jesus sends him instead as a missionary to the Decapolis.
verseByVerse.theology: The demons' name — 'Legion' — carries political resonance in a region under Roman military occupation. A legion is Rome's instrument of domination and terror. Whether intentional or not, the image that emerges is of demonic power operating in a way analogous to imperial power: occupying, dominating, destroying. Jesus confronts both kinds of power in the course of his ministry and defeats them both — the legion of demons in chapter 5, and Rome's instrument of execution in chapter 15. The victory over both is achieved in the same way: by going through, not around, the place of destruction.
verseByVerse.examples: The townspeople see a man delivered from years of torment, restored to himself, clothed, in his right mind — and they are afraid and ask Jesus to leave. This is one of the most haunting responses in the gospels. They preferred the known misery of the demoniac to the unknown implications of the one who cured him. Then: a Gentile town choosing the familiar nightmare over the unfamiliar grace. Now: every community that prefers the status quo to the disruption that genuine transformation always brings. Jesus does not force himself on those who ask him to leave. He gets in the boat. He sends the one man who wanted to go with him to tell what has happened. The gospel goes to the Decapolis not through a conquering army but through one restored man with a story.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit. He lived among the tombs. And no one could bind him anymore, not even with a chain… Night and day among the tombs and on the mountains he was always crying out and cutting himself with stones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The detail of this account — the unbreakable chains, the constant crying out, the self-harm, the habitation among the dead — is Peter's, who was there. It is not embellished for dramatic effect; it establishes the severity of the case so that the power of the deliverance is properly calibrated. Before Jesus arrives, the man runs to him and bows down. Even in his condition — perhaps especially in his condition — he is drawn to the one person who can help him. The demons recognize Jesus before any human in the region does: 'What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?'

The name 'Legion' and the begging of the demons not to be sent out of the region (v. 10) — and then into the pigs rather than into the abyss (cf. Luke 8:31) — reveals the demons' vulnerability even as they hold the man captive. They are not autonomous powers; they are subject to Jesus's authority and must negotiate for terms.

The name itself would have landed hard on Mark's first readers in Rome. A legion was a Roman army unit of some six thousand men — the empire's instrument of occupation, the thing that arrived in your district and stayed, that could not be resisted and would not leave. That is the word these spirits choose for themselves, and it describes exactly what they had done to this man: moved in, taken possession, held territory. So Mark sets two occupations side by side in his Gospel. There is the one everybody in that country could see, and there is the one nobody could do anything about — and Jesus walks up the beach and evicts the second with a sentence. He will deal with the first too, in his own way and at his own cost, when Rome nails him to a post outside Jerusalem and discovers it cannot hold him either. The pigs' rush into the sea is a vivid acted-out picture of what the demons were doing to the man: destroying him, driving him toward the sea, toward death. Their fate reveals their nature and their intention.

A reader with a map will notice a real puzzle. Mark calls this 'the country of the Gerasenes,' but Gerasa was a city some thirty miles from the lake — far too distant for a herd to run 'down the steep bank into the sea.' Matthew names the Gadarenes (Gadara, about six miles off, still not on the shore), and some manuscripts of all three Gospels read Gergesenes. The likely answer is that Gergesa (modern Kursi), a small place right on the eastern shore where the hills drop sharply to the water, was the actual spot; Gerasa and Gadara were the two well-known cities whose district reached down to that shore, and each writer named the region by the city his readers would recognize, much as one might say a village lies 'in greater London.' The steep bank is still there to be seen. What looks like a contradiction is the ordinary looseness of naming a place by its nearest famous city; the shoreline itself fits the story exactly.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man, the one who had had the legion, sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid… And he did not permit him but said to him, 'Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The townspeople's fear at the sight of the restored man is a psychological realism: something this far outside the categories of normal experience produces terror rather than gratitude. Two thousand pigs are dead in the sea. A man they have known as a wild, unchained menace is sitting quietly in conversation. The categories break. Fear is the natural first response to a power you cannot classify.

Jesus's refusal to let the man come with him and his commissioning of him as a missionary to the Decapolis is striking. Elsewhere in Mark, healed people are told to say nothing. This man — a Gentile, in Gentile territory — is told to go and tell. He is the gospel's first missionary to the nations, and he carries out his commission: 'he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him.' When Jesus returns to the Decapolis in chapter 7–8, he will be met with a prepared crowd. This man prepared them.

But what about the pigs — two thousand animals drowned, and someone's living with them? The question is worth facing honestly, for the town clearly felt the loss; it is part of why they beg Jesus to leave. Three things answer it. First, it was the demons, not Jesus, who drove the herd to its death; Jesus permitted their request, and in permitting it he let their true intention — destruction — show itself in the open. Second, the arithmetic of heaven is not the arithmetic of the market: one tormented man, restored to his mind and his family and sent out as a herald of mercy, is worth more than any number of swine. 'Of how much more value is a man than a sheep!' Jesus had said (Matt 12:12) — and a man than a pig. Third, the town's reaction exposes a terrible preference: presented with a neighbour raised from a living death and a hillside of dead livestock, they grieve the livestock and fear the Healer, and ask him to go. There are still people who would rather keep their pigs than lose their sins. The loss of the herd is the price of a soul, and to the mind of Christ it was no contest at all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–43 — Jairus's Daughter and the Woman with the Bleeding
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Markan sandwich: Jairus's request opens the episode (vv. 21–24), the woman with the bleeding occupies the middle (vv. 25–34), and then the story of Jairus's daughter resumes and concludes (vv. 35–43). The sandwich is not an accident of memory but a deliberate interpretive structure: the woman's story illuminates the daughter's, and the daughter's story illuminates the woman's. Both involve twelve years: the woman has been bleeding for twelve years; the daughter is twelve years old. Both involve the concept of being 'made well/saved' — the same Greek word used in both cases. Both involve touch: the woman touches Jesus's garment; Jesus takes the girl's hand.

The woman's story, embedded in the middle of Jairus's, is itself a theological commentary on what is happening. She receives healing by touching Jesus's garment in faith — anonymous, uninvited, from behind, in a crowd. Jesus insists on drawing her out, on making the healing personal rather than mechanical: 'Daughter, your faith has made you well.' By the time this conversation is finished, a messenger arrives from Jairus's house: 'Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?' The delay created by the woman's story has cost Jairus his daughter's life — or so it seems. Jesus's response to the messenger is the heart of the whole chapter: 'Do not fear, only believe.'
verseByVerse.theology: 'Do not fear, only believe' (v. 36) — this is Jesus's word in the face of death. It is not a word of comfort that pretends death is not real; it is a word of command that relativizes death in light of who is present. The word 'fear' is the same word used of the disciples' reaction to the storm (4:41) and of the townspeople's reaction to the demoniac's deliverance (5:15). Fear is the natural human response to power beyond our comprehension. Faith is the response Jesus is asking for — not the absence of fear but the choice to trust the one who is saying 'do not fear.' Only believe. Present tense, continuous action. Keep believing even now. Even in this.
verseByVerse.examples: The woman who had spent twelve years and all her money on doctors and grown worse rather than better reaches out in a crowd for the fringe of Jesus's garment. She expects nothing but a touch; she receives a conversation. Jesus will not let the healing be anonymous. He calls her forward not to shame her — she has done nothing wrong — but to give her something more than a physical cure: a personal word, a relationship, a 'Daughter.' Physical healing without the personal word is medicine; Jesus gives both. Then: a woman who had tried everything else finally trying Jesus, in secret, from behind. Now: every person who comes to Jesus as a last resort after exhausting all other options — and finds that the last resort is also the first and only real one.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side, a great crowd gathered about him, and he was beside the sea. Then came one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name, and seeing him, he fell at his feet and implored him earnestly, saying, 'My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Jairus is named — one of the rare cases in the healing narratives where the suppliant is identified. He is a ruler of the synagogue, a position of considerable social standing, and yet he falls at Jesus’s feet. Desperation has dissolved his dignity. His daughter — ‘my little daughter’ (to thygatrion mou — the diminutive is tender) — is at the point of death. He has come not with a theological question or a test but with a father’s raw panic: come, lay your hands on her, let her live. Jesus goes with him. No conditions, no delay, no preliminary discussion. The simplicity of that response — ‘and he went with him’ — is itself the gospel: Jesus goes where desperate faith brings him.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years… She had heard the reports about Jesus and came up behind him in the crowd and touched his garment. For she said, 'If I touch even his garments, I will be made well.' And immediately the flow of blood dried up… And Jesus, perceiving in himself that power had gone out from him, immediately turned about in the crowd and said, 'Who touched my garments?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman’s medical history is told with clinical detail: twelve years of bleeding, many physicians, all her financial resources spent, growing worse. This is not a situation that responded to human help. Her approach to Jesus is itself a picture of faith: she comes from behind (her bleeding made her ritually unclean, and touching others made them unclean; she has no right to approach openly); she touches only the fringe of his garment (the minimal contact she dares); and she expects that this minimal, unauthorized contact will be enough. It is.

Jesus’s question — ‘Who touched my garments?’ — astonishes the disciples. The crowd is pressing in on all sides; many people are physically touching him. But he distinguishes between the accidental physical contact of the crowd and the intentional, faith-driven touch of the woman. Power had gone out from him — this is not magic or mechanism; it is the personal, directed power of the Son of God responding to faith. The woman comes forward in fear and trembling and falls at his feet. He calls her ‘Daughter’ — the same word of intimate address he used to the paralytic (‘Son’) in chapter 2. She is not a case to be managed; she is a person to be known.

The interruption is intentional in Mark’s narrative design. Jairus is watching this exchange with his daughter dying at home. Every moment Jesus spends on this woman is a moment closer to being too late. The delay is not a mistake in the story; it is a test. And the test comes immediately: ‘Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?’ (v. 35). The healing of the woman in the crowd is preparation for Jairus — the lesson in faith that he needed before his faith would be required at its most extreme.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, there came from the ruler's house some who said, 'Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?' But overhearing what they said, Jesus said to the ruler of the synagogue, 'Do not fear, only believe.'… And taking the child by the hand he said to her, 'Talitha cumi,' which means, 'Little girl, I say to you, arise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The messenger's words — 'Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?' — represent the world's verdict on the situation. Death is the end; beyond it, nothing remains to be done. Jesus overhears and addresses Jairus directly: 'Do not fear, only believe.' Not 'don't worry, I'll take care of it' — but 'do not fear' (stop the fear-response) and 'only believe' (keep the faith-response going). These are commands, not reassurances. Jesus is asking Jairus to hold a position that the facts around him do not support.

At the house Jesus says something that has been seized on ever since: ‘The child is not dead but sleeping’ — and the mourners laugh at him. Sceptics take the words at face value: she was never really dead, only in a coma or a faint, so this is no resurrection at all but a lucky misdiagnosis. But the reading collapses the moment you look at it. Everyone present was certain she had died — the messengers reported it, and the house was already full of professional mourners wailing and playing the flute, who are not hired for the unconscious; these were people who made their living recognising death, and they laughed precisely because they knew a corpse when they saw one. Mark, Matthew, and Luke all frame it as a raising, and Luke — a physician — states plainly that ‘her spirit returned’ (Luke 8:55). ‘Sleeping’ is not Jesus offering a second opinion on her pulse. It is his settled way of speaking about the death of those he intends to raise: of Lazarus, four days in the tomb and stinking, he said ‘our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep’, and when they misunderstood he told them plainly, ‘Lazarus has died’ (John 11:11–14); Paul calls dead believers those who ‘have fallen asleep’ (1 Thess 4:13–14; 1 Cor 15:20). So the word is not a smaller claim but a far larger one. To the mourners death was final; to the One standing in the room it was as temporary as a night’s sleep, and waking this dead girl would cost him no more effort than a parent leaning over a bed in the morning. He does not deny that she died. He announces that death, in his presence, has just become something you get up from.

The Aramaic words 'Talitha cumi' — preserved in Mark because this is Peter's memory of exactly what Jesus said — mean simply 'Little girl, arise.' The simplicity is devastating. No elaborate ritual, no lengthy prayer, no dramatic gesture. Just two words in a dead child's ear. And she gets up and walks. Jesus's instructions to give her something to eat are a mark of practical tenderness: she has been ill; she needs food. And the 'strict orders' to tell no one — the Messianic Secret again — are almost comically impossible; you cannot hide a resurrection. The secret will not hold. The truth of who Jesus is refuses to be contained.

5.theology:
Chapter 5 is an exposition of divine power encountering human hopelessness at its most extreme. The demoniac: beyond human restraint, living in death, a danger to himself and others — restored and commissioned. The woman: beyond medical help, ritually excluded, financially ruined — healed and called 'Daughter.' Jairus's daughter: beyond any help at all, dead — raised and given something to eat. The three together argue that there is no situation — however long it has lasted, however many human remedies have failed, however final the pronouncement — that lies outside the authority of the Son of God.

The chapter also teaches us something about how Jesus works. He does not process people in bulk. He stops for the woman in the crowd. He takes only three disciples and the parents into the room with the dead girl. He speaks her name in her own language. He asks for food to be given to her. The God who raises the dead also attends to the lunch that follows. Power and tenderness are not in tension in this chapter; they are the same thing.
5.examples: Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue, falls at Jesus's feet and begs him for his daughter's life — and then waits, at the back of the crowd, while Jesus stops for an unnamed woman's problem. Every minute of the delay is a minute closer to the verdict 'she is dead.' The faith that 'Do not fear, only believe' requires is not the faith of a comfortable moment; it is the faith that keeps trusting while the worst is happening, while the messengers are arriving with bad news, while every second of waiting makes the outcome less likely. This is the faith that pleases God — not the faith that believes when the evidence supports it, but the faith that believes when the evidence says 'stop.' Then: Jairus, ruler of a synagogue, watching Jesus stop. Now: every parent who has waited in a hospital corridor while everything moved in the wrong direction. The word is the same: do not fear. Only believe.

6.title: Rejection, Mission, Death, and Bread
6.text: "And he took the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to heaven, he blessed and broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the people. And he divided the two fish among them all." (Mark 6:41 ESV)
6.overview:
Chapter 6 is the most varied chapter in Mark — it contains a rejection, a mission, a murder, a feeding miracle, and a water-walking. These are not loosely collected stories; they are arranged to tell a single larger story about the reception of the gospel and the nature of the one who brings it. The rejection at Nazareth (vv. 1–6) frames everything: even the hometown crowd, those who watched him grow up, cannot see what is right in front of them. Familiarity with Jesus, Mark implies, is no guarantee of faith. The mission of the Twelve (vv. 7–13) is the response to rejection: if Nazareth will not receive the word, the disciples will take it everywhere else.

The death of John the Baptist (vv. 14–29), inserted between the sending-out and the return of the Twelve, is a dark parenthesis that tells us where the kingdom is heading. John is the forerunner not only of Jesus's ministry but of Jesus's death: rejected, imprisoned, beheaded at the whim of a vain king and a vengeful woman. The feeding of the five thousand and the walking on water that close the chapter swing back to the demonstration of power — but the disciples still do not understand. 'Their hearts were hardened' (v. 52). The pattern of chapter 4 holds: hearing does not automatically produce understanding.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — Rejection, Mission, and the Death of John
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The rejection at Nazareth is painful precisely because it is so ordinary. The people who watched Jesus grow up are offended at his teaching — they know his family, they know his occupation (carpenter — the only time this word is applied to Jesus in the gospels), they know his brothers and sisters. Their knowledge of his background makes genuine faith in him seem absurd. 'A prophet is not without honour, except in his hometown and among his relatives and in his own household' — this principle extends beyond literal hometowns to any situation where proximity has produced familiarity and familiarity has killed wonder.

The death of John the Baptist is told with remarkable narrative skill — a banquet, a dance, a rash oath, a vengeful request. Herod is not a monster; he is a weak man caught between his genuine fear of John, his public oath, and his social humiliation. The machinery of political power in the service of personal vengeance produces one of the most unjust deaths in the gospel narrative. The forerunner is beheaded in a dungeon so that a king does not lose face at a birthday party.
verseByVerse.theology: The mission of the Twelve (vv. 7–13) is the first extension of Jesus's own ministry through human agents. Two by two — the minimum number for legal witness and practical support — they go out with authority over unclean spirits, preaching repentance, anointing the sick with oil. The instruction to take nothing for the journey (no bag, no bread, no money, no extra tunic) is not asceticism but a demonstration of dependence: the missionary is to depend entirely on the hospitality of those who receive the message. The shaking of dust from the feet at rejection (v. 11) is a solemn gesture borrowed from Jewish practice when leaving Gentile territory — it says 'we have brought what was ours to bring; the responsibility now rests with you.' The gospel creates both welcome and accountability.
verseByVerse.examples: Herod, who had heard John 'gladly' and 'kept him safe' and 'was greatly perplexed' but listened to him (v. 20) — and still had him killed — is one of the gospel's most searching portraits. He was moved by the gospel; he was not transformed by it. He heard gladly without repenting genuinely. The gladness without repentance is perhaps the most dangerous spiritual condition: it provides the feeling of religiosity without the reality of conversion. Then: a king who listened to a prophet and refused to be changed by what he heard. Now: every hearer of the gospel who is genuinely moved in church on Sunday and genuinely unchanged by Monday. Herod is the rocky ground of chapter 4 given a name and a palace.

verseByVerse.quote: And on the Sabbath he began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard him were astonished, saying, 'Where did this man get these things? What is the wisdom given to him? How are such mighty works done by his hands? Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Nazareth synagogue crowd asks the right questions and draws the wrong conclusion. They are astonished — same word as the Capernaum crowd in chapter 1 — but their astonishment becomes a stumbling block rather than an invitation to faith. They cannot move from 'where did he get this?' to the answer because the answer requires accepting that someone they watched build furniture is the Son of God. The scandal of incarnation is not merely theological; it is domestic. The Word became flesh in a specific house, in a specific trade, in a specific family. And the specific family knows too much to worship.

'They took offence at him' (v. 3) — the word is the one from which we get 'scandal.' He was a skandalon to them — a stumbling block, a trap. His familiarity was the trap. Mark notes that he 'could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them' (v. 5) — a deliberately arresting statement. His power was not diminished, but the context of unbelief limited what he chose to do. Faith is not the mechanism that generates the miracle, but it is the context in which Jesus ordinarily works.

Mark names them where Matthew only lists them: 'the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon,' and 'his sisters' too. A reader is bound to ask whether these are Jesus's real siblings. The question has divided the church. Rome and the Orthodox, holding that Mary remained a virgin all her life, take them as cousins (so Jerome) or as children of Joseph by an earlier marriage (so the Orthodox). But the words mean most naturally what they say: these are the later sons and daughters of Joseph and Mary, Jesus's younger half-brothers and half-sisters, born in the ordinary way. Matthew says Joseph 'knew her not until' she had borne her son (Matt 1:25), and calls Jesus her 'firstborn' — a word that quietly waits for others to follow. Mary's honour is not a lifelong virginity but that she bore and raised the Son of God and then mothered his brothers. And there is gospel gold in that little family list. During his ministry these brothers did not believe in him — 'not even his brothers believed in him' (John 7:5), and here in Nazareth they are among the offended. Yet after the resurrection we find them in the upper room praying (Acts 1:14); James becomes the pillar of the Jerusalem church and writes the letter that bears his name; Jude writes another. What turns a scornful younger brother into a man who signs himself 'a servant of the Lord Jesus Christ'? Only an empty tomb. The unbelief of Jesus's own brothers, and their later devotion to the death, is one of the quiet, powerful evidences that he rose.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the twelve and began to send them out two by two, and gave them authority over the unclean spirits. He charged them to take nothing for their journey except a staff — no bag, no bread, no money in their belts — but to wear sandals and not put on two tunics.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sending of the Twelve is the first extension of Jesus's own mission through human agents. The authority he gives them is real — authority over unclean spirits — not a delegation of reduced power but a genuine commissioning. The instruction to take nothing for the journey creates a structural dependence on hospitality: the missionary relies on the community he serves, which creates both relationship and accountability on both sides. The instruction to stay in one house when welcomed (v. 10) prevents the social climbing that would undermine the message: you accept what is offered and stay.

One detail in the list has been a favourite of sceptics for centuries, and a reader with Matthew open will spot it at once. Mark says take a staff and wear sandals; Matthew has Jesus forbid both — no staff, no sandals (Matt 10:9-10); and Luke too says take no staff (Luke 9:3). It looks like a flat contradiction over the smallest of things, and it dissolves the moment the verbs are examined. Matthew's word is acquire — do not procure, do not get hold of; Mark's is take, in the sense of carry along. Put them together and one plain instruction stands behind both: do not equip yourselves for this journey. Do not go shopping for a new staff or a spare pair of sandals; go exactly as you are, with the stick already in your hand and the sandals already on your feet, and take nothing extra. Every traveller in that country owned a staff and wore sandals; neither writer is debating whether a man may walk shod. They are both forbidding the same thing — provisioning — which is the whole point of the paragraph. Matthew forbids the shopping trip; Mark permits the walking stick. The apparent collision, looked at closely, turns out to be two men describing one scene from two sides.

The disciples go, preach repentance, cast out many demons, and anoint many sick with oil who are healed. The apostolic mission is a continuation of Jesus's own — the same preaching, the same exorcism, the same healing. What the disciples do in chapter 6 they cannot do in chapter 9 (the epileptic boy). The difference will be identified by Jesus: 'This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer' (9:29). Power without ongoing dependence on Jesus becomes power that fails.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was Herod who had sent and seized John and bound him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, because he had married her. For John had been saying to Herod, 'It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod Antipas (son of Herod the Great) had divorced his first wife and married Herodias, who had divorced his half-brother Philip. John the Baptist confronted this marriage directly: 'It is not lawful for you.' He lost his freedom and eventually his head for saying so. The prophetic courage of John's confrontation — speaking truth to power at personal cost — stands as a model and a warning throughout church history. The prophet who prophesies only what the king wants to hear is not a prophet; he is a courtier.

The birthday banquet scene is told with almost novelistic detail: the dance, the oath ('whatever you ask, up to half my kingdom' — a grandiose formula of generosity that Herod did not intend to be taken literally), the consultation with the mother, the terrible request. Herod is 'exceedingly sorry' — but public shame before his guests matters more than justice for a prophet.

And Mark has told us something about this king that makes the beheading worse rather than better. Herod feared John, knowing him to be a righteous and holy man, and kept him safe; when he heard him he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly (v. 20). Gladly. He enjoyed the preaching. He came back for more of it. He protected the preacher from a wife who wanted him dead. Everything was there except the one thing that matters — he would not repent, and a man who will not repent will eventually kill the voice that keeps asking him to. Herod is the most unsettling portrait in this chapter precisely because he is not a scoffer. He is the rocky ground of the parable two chapters back, given a name and a palace: the word received with real interest, real feeling, even real pleasure, and no root. Being moved by a sermon is not the same thing as being changed by it, and Herod's platter is the proof. He sends the executioner. The head arrives on a platter. John's disciples come and take the body and lay it in a tomb — a quiet prefiguring of what will happen to their master's body in chapter 15.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–56 — The Feeding, the Walking, and the Healings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The return of the Twelve and the retreat that follows is interrupted by the crowd — who run ahead on foot and arrive before the boat. Jesus sees the crowd and is moved with compassion, 'because they were like sheep without a shepherd' — an Old Testament image (Num. 27:17; 1 Kgs. 22:17; Ezek. 34) for a people without adequate leadership. He begins to teach them. Late in the day, the disciples want to send them away to find food. Jesus says: you give them something to eat. They have five loaves and two fish. He takes them, looks up to heaven, blesses and breaks them, and feeds five thousand men. The number of baskets of leftovers — twelve — is surely intentional: one for each of the Twelve, one for each tribe of the new Israel.

The walking on water (vv. 45–52) follows the same pattern as the storm of chapter 4: the disciples are terrified by what they see, Jesus reassures them, the storm stills, and Mark notes that 'they were utterly astounded, for they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened.' The feeding should have told them something about who he is. It did not. The walking on water should have told them something more. It did not. Mark's honest portrayal of the disciples' persistent incomprehension is one of the most reliable signs of the gospel's authenticity: no church invents this portrait of its founders.
verseByVerse.theology: The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle of Jesus (apart from the resurrection) that appears in all four gospels, and in John it is the occasion for the Bread of Life discourse. The Eucharistic echoes — 'he blessed and broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the people' (v. 41) — are unmistakable. This is not the Last Supper; it is an anticipation of it, and of every Lord's Table since. The one who feeds five thousand with five loaves continues to feed his people through the same broken bread. The abundance that left twelve baskets of fragments points to a kingdom where the resources of the King never run out.
verseByVerse.examples: When the disciples say 'Send them away to go into the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat,' Jesus's response is 'You give them something to eat.' They object on grounds of arithmetic: two hundred denarii would not be enough to buy bread for this crowd. Jesus is not asking them to solve the problem with their own resources; he is asking them to bring what they have and let him do the rest. The five loaves and two fish are an embarrassingly small response to the problem — but they are the right response, because the multiplication happens in his hands, not theirs. Then: disciples doing arithmetic in front of a hungry crowd. Now: every pastor or leader facing a need that is obviously larger than their resources, hearing the same word — 'you give them something to eat.' Bring what you have. What he makes of it is his business.

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles returned to Jesus and told him all that they had done and taught. And he said to them, 'Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while.'… When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And he began to teach them many things… 'You give them something to eat.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles return from their mission full of what they have done and taught. Jesus quietly redirects them: come away and rest. The rhythm of mission and withdrawal is built into his own pattern from 1:35. But the rest does not come — the crowd runs ahead and meets them on the shore. Jesus’s response to the interruption of his own plan for rest is one of the most revealing moments in the gospel: ‘he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd.’

The ‘sheep without a shepherd’ image carries the whole prophetic tradition. Ezekiel 34 mourns shepherds who scatter and destroy the flock; Numbers 27:17 uses the identical phrase when Moses prays for a leader so Israel will not be ‘as sheep that have no shepherd.’ Jesus looks at the crowd and sees, behind the faces, the ancient pastoral failure — leaders who have left the people without genuine care. His compassion expresses itself first not in miracle but in word: he began to teach them many things. He feeds the soul before he feeds the body.

By evening the disciples propose the obvious solution: send them away to buy food. Jesus turns the responsibility back: ‘You give them something to eat.’ They take him literally — two hundred denarii, most of a year’s wages. Jesus is not asking for an economic calculation; he is pressing the question of trust. What do you have? Five loaves and two fish. Bring them to me.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to heaven, he blessed and broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the people. And he divided the two fish among them all. And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and of the fish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus instructs the crowd to sit down ‘on the green grass’ — one of Mark’s specific eyewitness details, the spring green of Palestinian pastureland, a detail only Peter could supply. The crowd arranged in groups of fifty and a hundred recalls Israel encamped in the wilderness — Moses-typology is deliberate: the wilderness, the bread from heaven, the organized camps. This is the new Exodus, and the one who feeds them is greater than Moses, who only reported that the manna had arrived.

The gestures — looking up to heaven, blessing, breaking, giving — will be repeated at the Last Supper (14:22) and recognized at Emmaus (Luke 24:30). Mark is preparing his reader: the one who feeds thousands in the wilderness will give his own body as bread for the world. ‘They all ate and were satisfied’ — echortasthēsan, eaten to fullness. Twelve baskets of fragments remained — more left over than they started with. The disciples who had nothing to give each carry a basket of the surplus. This is the arithmetic of the kingdom: five loaves in the hands of Christ become abundance for thousands, with excess for all.

verseByVerse.quote: And he saw that they were making headway painfully, for the wind was against them. And about the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them… And he got into the boat with them, and the wind ceased. And they were utterly astounded.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus has gone up the mountain to pray — the disciples are on the lake in the dark, rowing against the wind. The fourth watch is 3–6 AM: they have been at it for hours. He comes to them walking on the water, and he 'meant to pass by them' — a phrase with deep Old Testament roots. When the Lord 'passes by' in Exodus 33:22 and 1 Kings 19:11, it is a theophany, a revelation of divine presence and glory. Jesus is not trying to sneak past them; he is revealing himself in a manner saturated with the language of God's self-disclosure.

Their terror produces a cry, Jesus reassures them ('It is I' — the divine name, ego eimi), and he gets into the boat. The wind ceases. Mark's comment that they were 'utterly astounded' and that 'they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened' is devastating in its honesty. The feeding should have taught them who he is. The walking should have reinforced it. Both events are beyond the categories of the merely remarkable; both require the category of Creator and Lord. But hardness of heart can outlast even direct encounter with the miraculous.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored to the shore. And when they got out of the boat, the people immediately recognized him and ran about the whole region and began to bring the sick people on their mats to wherever they heard he was.
verseByVerse.commentary: The landing at Gennesaret produces an immediate crowd response — people running from all over the region, carrying the sick on mats, placing them wherever Jesus is. The detail that 'as many as touched even the fringe of his garment were made well' (v. 56) echoes the woman with the bleeding in chapter 5, generalizing her experience: the healing power available to her anonymous faith-touch is available to the whole region. The fringe of his garment — the tzitzit, the ritual tassels worn by observant Jewish men — was believed to carry some connection to the power of the one who wore it. Jesus does not correct this popular belief; he lets the healings happen. The crowds are not theologians; they are sick people reaching for the nearest point of contact with the one who can help. He honours the reach.

6.theology: Chapter 6 argues implicitly for the inexhaustibility of Jesus's power and the persistence of human unbelief. He feeds thousands and the disciples' hearts are still hardened. He walks on water and they are still astonished rather than worshipping. The chapter does not present this as a mystery to be solved but as a reality to be acknowledged: the gap between miracle and faith is not closed by more miracles. Faith is a gift, not a conclusion. The disciples who saw everything in chapters 1–6 still do not understand. It will take three more years of being with him, and then a cross and an empty tomb, before the pieces fall into place.
6.examples: The compassion of Jesus for the crowd in verse 34 is expressed in a specific image: 'they were like sheep without a shepherd.' This is a pastoral metaphor — not primarily about individuals but about communities. Whole communities can be without adequate spiritual leadership, drifting and confused and vulnerable, not because they are unimportant but because no one has taken the responsibility of shepherd. Jesus's response to the shepherd-less crowd is not to organize a programme — it is to teach them. The primary ministry of the shepherd is not administration but the word. Then: a crowd running ahead of the boat to meet Jesus, bringing the sick on mats. Now: the local church — whether small or large — as the community where the hungry are fed, the sick are brought, and the shepherd who gives his life for the sheep is at the centre.

7.title: Clean and Unclean: What Really Defiles
7.text: "'There is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him, but the things that come out of a person are what defile him.'" (Mark 7:15 ESV)
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is a turning point in the geography of Mark's gospel. The controversy about clean and unclean (vv. 1–23) is the last major engagement with the Pharisees before Jesus moves decisively into Gentile territory. The two healings that follow — the Syrophoenician woman (vv. 24–30) and the deaf and mute man (vv. 31–37) — both take place outside Israel. The sequence is not accidental: once Jesus has declared all foods clean and exposed the tradition of the elders as a human addition to the word of God, the boundaries of the clean and the unclean community are redefined. The gospel can move to the Gentiles because the gospel always was for the Gentiles — the tradition of the elders was the obstacle, not the law of God.

The saying of v. 15 — 'nothing outside a person can defile him, but the things that come out of a person are what defile him' — is one of the most radical statements Jesus makes in the gospels. Mark notes in v. 19 that 'he declared all foods clean.' This is not a minor adjustment; it is the abolition of one of the most distinctive markers of Jewish identity. The author of this declaration is the same one who gave the food laws at Sinai. He is now fulfilling what they always pointed toward: it is the human heart, not the human diet, that is the source of defilement.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Tradition, the Word of God, and the Human Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem observe the disciples eating with 'defiled hands' — unwashed, not in the ceremonial sense of hygiene but in the ritual sense of tradition. Mark explains this for his Roman audience (v. 3–4): the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat unless they wash their hands ceremonially, and there are many other traditions they observe. This explanation flags that Mark is writing for people who do not know these customs, confirming the Roman destination of the gospel.

Jesus's confrontation with the tradition of the elders is a confrontation about the source and authority of religious obligation. The tradition of the elders — the Oral Torah, later codified in the Mishnah — was understood by the Pharisees as having equal authority with the Written Torah, both given to Moses at Sinai. Jesus denies this flatly: it is human tradition, not the commandment of God. And he demonstrates with a specific example — the Corban vow — how the tradition had become a mechanism for evading the actual commandments of God.
verseByVerse.theology: The Corban example (vv. 9–13) is precise and damning. Corban was a vow by which a person could declare their property dedicated to God, effectively making it unavailable for any other purpose — including the support of aging parents. The fifth commandment required honouring father and mother; the Corban vow created a legal mechanism by which the letter of piety could be used to violate the spirit of the commandment. Jesus identifies this as 'making void the word of God by your tradition.' The religious apparatus designed to honour God had become, in this specific application, a tool for dishonoring it. The critique applies to every religious tradition that generates a system of obligation parallel to Scripture and then uses that system to evade Scripture's actual demands.
verseByVerse.examples: The list of things that come from within (vv. 21–22) is not an exhaustive catalogue but a representative sample: sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. What they have in common is their origin: 'from within, out of the heart of man.' The Pharisaic tradition had focused enormous energy on external purity — the cleanliness of hands and cups and pots. Jesus directs the focus entirely inward: the problem is not the contamination that comes from outside but the corruption that originates within. This is the anthropology that makes the gospel necessary: the human heart is not essentially good, requiring only the removal of external influences. It is essentially bent, requiring radical renewal from within. Only the new birth can produce a new heart.

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees and some of the scribes gathered to him, having come from Jerusalem… 'Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites, as it is written, "This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men."'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The accusation that the disciples eat with 'defiled' (unwashed) hands opens a controversy that goes far beyond table manners. The tradition of the elders required ritual handwashing before meals as an extension of the purity laws governing priests. The Pharisees had applied priestly requirements to all Israel, effectively making every Jewish meal a quasi-priestly act. The intention was honourable; the problem was the status given to the tradition — equal to or exceeding the commandment of God.

Jesus's citation of Isaiah 29:13 identifies the problem precisely: the heart is far from God while the lips and the external observances are perfectly maintained. This is not hypocrisy in the popular sense of conscious pretence; it is something more subtle — the substitution of religious performance for genuine relational devotion. You can maintain the tradition flawlessly and simultaneously be miles from God. The tradition was designed to keep you close; when it becomes a substitute for closeness, it has inverted its own purpose.

Then Jesus makes it concrete with a scandalous example, and it turns on a word Mark leaves untranslated: 'Corban.' To pronounce something Corban was to declare it dedicated to God — set apart, off-limits for ordinary use, as if placed on the temple altar. The scribes taught that such a vow was binding and irreversible. Here is how it was abused. A man with aging parents, legally bound by the fifth commandment to support them, could look at the money he owed their care and declare it 'Corban' — vowed to God. Now, said the tradition, his hands were tied: the money was sacred; he could not spend it on father or mother. Yet in practice he often never handed it to the temple at all; he simply kept the use of it himself, shielded from his duty by a holy-sounding word. So a rule invented to honour God became a device for robbing parents — and doing it with a straight face, in God's name. This is Isaiah 29:13 made flesh: the lips say 'devoted to God' while the heart abandons the people God commanded them to love. 'You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men.'

verseByVerse.quote: 'There is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him, but the things that come out of a person are what defile him.'… 'For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The saying of v. 15, addressed to the crowd, is deliberately public and maximally provocative: it overturns a foundational principle of Jewish purity law. Nothing that enters from outside defiles; defilement comes from within. Mark's parenthetical comment in v. 19 — 'thus he declared all foods clean' — is one of the most significant editorial notes in the New Testament. Jesus is not merely winning a debate about handwashing; he is abolishing the food laws as a boundary marker between clean and unclean people. The implications for Gentile inclusion are enormous and will be worked out in Acts 10 (Peter's vision) and Acts 15 (the Jerusalem Council).

The private explanation to the disciples (vv. 17–23) unpacks the anthropology: the source of defilement is the human heart, from which emerge twelve specific expressions of corruption. This is not Pelagian optimism about human nature receiving a minor correction from religion; it is a diagnosis of radical corruption requiring a radical remedy. The gospel addresses the source: 'I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you' (Ezek. 36:26). External purity regulations treat the symptom; the new birth addresses the disease.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–37 — Two Healings Beyond Israel's Borders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having declared all foods clean and dissolved one of the primary boundary markers between Jews and Gentiles, Jesus moves into Gentile territory. The two healings of vv. 24–37 both occur outside Israel — one in the region of Tyre (Phoenicia), one in the Decapolis — and both involve Gentiles. The sequence is theologically deliberate: the teaching of vv. 1–23 has cleared the ground; the healings of vv. 24–37 demonstrate the extension of the kingdom to those who had been outside its boundaries.

The Syrophoenician woman episode (vv. 24–30) is one of the most difficult in the gospels and the most misread.
